raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure and left ventricular systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, when no alternative cause is evident [1]. Contemporary definitions no longer require left ventricular dilation and generally use left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% as the key imaging criterion [2,3]. PPCM remains clinically important because pregnancy-related dyspnea, edema, and fatigue can mimic normal gestation, delaying recognition until pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, or sudden death occurs [4–6].

Reported incidence varies markedly by geography and ascertainment. Early U.S. discharge data suggested approximately 1 case per 3,189 live births [9], whereas later U.S. population analyses found increasing rates and substantial in-hospital morbidity [8]. Incidence is higher in women of African ancestry and in regions such as sub-Saharan Africa and Haiti [29]. Established risk factors include Black race, older maternal age, multiparity, multifetal gestation, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and pre-eclampsia [7,10,26]. PPCM can also cluster with familial dilated cardiomyopathy, indicating that pregnancy may unmask latent genetic susceptibility [21,22].

Pathogenesis is best conceptualized as a “two-hit” process: late-pregnancy vascular/hormonal stress superimposed on host vulnerability [5,6]. A seminal murine model linked cardiomyocyte STAT3 deficiency to oxidative stress, cathepsin-D activation, cleavage of prolactin into an antiangiogenic 16-kDa fragment, endothelial injury, and postpartum cardiomyopathy [18]. Downstream, 16-kDa prolactin induces endothelial microRNA-146a, which can be transferred to cardiomyocytes and impair metabolic and survival pathways [20]. A parallel angiogenic model showed that impaired cardiac PGC-1α/VEGF signaling and excess placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), particularly in pre-eclampsia or multifetal pregnancy, can produce systolic dysfunction [19]. These mechanisms align with clinical biomarker data linking vascular mediators to symptoms and outcomes [13].

Diagnosis requires high suspicion in any late-pregnancy or postpartum patient with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, persistent tachycardia, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, or disproportionate exercise intolerance. Initial evaluation includes electrocardiography, natriuretic peptides, chest imaging when indicated, and echocardiography to document LVEF, chamber size, valve disease, right ventricular function, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [3,11]. Cardiac magnetic resonance can clarify myocarditis, scar, thrombus, and alternative diagnoses, though gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy unless essential [14]. Troponin elevation and low initial LVEF predict persistent dysfunction in several cohorts [15,30].

Prognosis is heterogeneous. In the prospective North American IPAC cohort, many women improved substantially over 12 months, but severe baseline LV dysfunction, LV dilation, and Black race were associated with lower recovery and more adverse events [12]. Earlier echocardiographic studies similarly showed that lower LVEF and larger LV dimensions identify patients at risk for incomplete recovery [16,17]. Right-sided involvement, high sFlt1, thrombus, and delayed diagnosis further worsen risk [13,14]. Because recovery may continue beyond 6–12 months, durable devices or transplantation should be reserved for refractory shock or persistent advanced heart failure after appropriate stabilization.

Management combines pregnancy-safe acute heart failure care, guideline-directed postpartum therapy, anticoagulation when indicated, and multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric planning. During pregnancy, loop diuretics, beta-blockers, hydralazine, nitrates, and digoxin may be used cautiously; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally deferred until after delivery because of fetal or lactation safety concerns [2,3]. Postpartum, standard heart failure therapy should be rapidly optimized. Anticoagulation is considered with LVEF ≤30–35%, atrial fibrillation, LV thrombus, bromocriptine use, or other thrombotic risk factors, recognizing pregnancy and puerperium as hypercoagulable states [3].

Disease-specific therapy remains an evolving area. Pentoxifylline improved outcomes in an early South African randomized study, supporting an inflammatory component, but it is not standard therapy [25]. Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin release, improved outcomes in a small proof-of-concept trial and was associated with high recovery rates in a German randomized study comparing short versus longer treatment regimens, although neither trial established definitive mortality benefit [23,24]. If bromocriptine is used, breastfeeding stops and thromboprophylaxis is recommended [3].

Counseling about future pregnancy is central. Subsequent pregnancy carries relapse risk, especially when LVEF remains abnormal before conception [27]. Even women with apparent recovery can relapse, requiring shared decision-making, preconception echocardiography, medication review, and close surveillance during pregnancy and postpartum [28]. Overall, earlier diagnosis, standardized cardio-obstetric pathways, genetic evaluation in selected patients, and trials of targeted therapies are the priorities for reducing persistent heart failure and maternal mortality in PPCM.
